User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm single, live in San Diego CA. My employer Desert Sun Logistics paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 3 clients, got $890 interest from Marcus savings account and $480 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Thanks for laying this out clearly. Here’s what’s likely deductible for 2023 and how to report it, plus the best approach given your facts.

What’s deductible (federal)
- Side gig (graphic design – Schedule C):
  - $780 in business supplies (if for the freelance work; not deductible if for your W‑2 job).
  - Home office for the freelance business (see “Home office” below).
  - Self-employment tax (you pay it on your Schedule C profit) and you get an above-the-line deduction for half of it.
  - You may also get the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (roughly 20% of your net freelance income, subject to limits; computed on Form 8995).
- Student loan interest: Up to $2,500, but it phases out for single filers with MAGI $75,000–$90,000 in 2023. Based on your numbers, you’re near the top of the phase-out, so you’ll only get a small deduction (roughly ~$100–$150 if all else holds). You’ll need Form 1098‑E.
- Charitable contributions ($720 to Northwest Harvest): Deductible only if you itemize. For 2023 there’s no above-the-line charitable deduction.
- Interest ($890) and dividends ($480): Not deductible; they’re taxable income. Some or all dividends may be “qualified” and taxed at lower rates—check 1099‑DIV boxes 1a/1b.

Standard deduction vs. itemizing (single, 2023)
- Standard deduction: $13,850.
- Itemizing: With no mortgage interest and as a renter, your typical itemized items are:
  - State and local taxes (SALT) up to $10,000 cap, plus
  - Charitable gifts ($720)
  - Medical only if over 7.5% of AGI (not indicated).
- Given your profile, itemizing is unlikely to exceed $13,850. Standard deduction is probably better.

Home office (for your freelance business only)
- Requirements: Regular and exclusive business use, and it’s your principal place of business for the freelance work. Using the space for your W‑2 job doesn’t qualify for an employee deduction (those are suspended), but it doesn’t break “exclusive” as long as the space isn’t used personally. You must allocate the deduction to the freelance activity—if the room is used for both W‑2 and freelance, prorate by time used for the freelance work.
- Your space: 165 sq ft out of 850 sq ft = 19.4% of home.
- Methods:
  - Simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 165 × $5 = $825 deduction (no depreciation, no carryforward).
  - Actual expense method: Deduct 19.4% of indirect home costs. With rent $2,100/mo ($25,200/yr), rent portion = about $4,893 before any time-use proration. If, say, 60% of the office time was for your freelance work, you’d deduct 60% of $4,893 ≈ $2,936. This deduction can’t create a loss (excess may carry forward when using Form 8829).
- Which to pick: If you used the office mostly for the freelance business, the actual method will likely yield a much bigger deduction than the $825 simplified method.

Where everything goes (key federal forms)
- Form 1040
  - Line 1: W‑2 wages ($84,900).
  - Line 2b: Interest ($890). Use Schedule B only if total interest+ordinary dividends > $1,500 or other special situations.
  - Lines 3a/3b: Qualified/ordinary dividends ($480 per 1099‑DIV).
  - Line 13: Qualified Business Income deduction (from Form 8995), if applicable.
- Schedule C (sole prop – graphic design): Report $8,900 income, claim $780 supplies, and your home office (line 30 if simplified; otherwise attach Form 8829).
- Form 8829 (if using actual home office): Compute and flow the allowed home office deduction to Schedule C.
- Schedule SE: Compute self-employment tax on your Schedule C profit; half of this becomes an above-the-line deduction on Schedule 1.
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments to Income):
  - Deductible part of self-employment tax.
  - Student loan interest deduction (limited and phased out as noted).
- Schedule B: Only if required (see above).
- Form 8995: QBI deduction (likely small but worth taking if eligible).
- Schedule A: Only if you itemize (likely not beneficial this year).

Rough planning notes based on your figures
- Freelance profit before home office: $8,900 − $780 = $8,120.
- Actual-method home office (before any time allocation): ≈ $4,893. If all office time is for freelancing, you could likely deduct the full amount (limited to not creating a net loss).
- Using the actual method will reduce your Schedule C profit substantially and lower both income tax and self-employment tax. The simplified method ($825) is easier but likely less favorable for you.

To confirm and optimize, could you clarify:
- Were the $780 supplies for your freelance work (and not reimbursed by your employer)?
- Is the 165 sq ft office used exclusively for business, and approximately what share of its use time is for your freelance work versus your W‑2 job?
- Did you receive 1099‑NEC forms from your clients, and Forms 1099‑INT and 1099‑DIV from Marcus/Fidelity? Do you have a 1098‑E for student loan interest?
- Any other deductible business expenses (software, subscriptions, internet portion, equipment, professional fees)?

Once I have those, I can fine-tune the home office calculation and your expected deductions.
